system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2167-03-12 16:32:00 to 2167-03-16 16:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with acute myeloid leukemia in remission following double cord blood transplant, was admitted with severe diffuse joint pain and painful, infected toes. He had recently been hospitalized for Stenotrophomonas bacteremia and incomplete antibiotic treatment due to renal issues. On admission, he was found to have MRSA infection in his left big toe, which was treated with IV vancomycin and excisional debridement. His severe arthralgias, unresponsive to prior therapies, resolved completely after increasing his prednisone dose, supporting a diagnosis of graft-versus-host disease. Renal function improved with supportive care, and hyperkalemia resolved with Kayexelate. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic completion. He was discharged home in stable condition with a plan for tapering steroids, continued vancomycin, and follow-up with transplant and podiatry teams.
problems: MRSA infection of left first digit
Herpes simplex without mention of complication
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
TYPE OF EXAMINATION:  Chest AP portable single view.

INDICATION:  One year status post bone marrow transplant, now new onset of
fever, evaluate for possible pneumonia.

FINDINGS:  AP single view of the chest has been obtained with patient in
upright position and analysis is performed in direct comparison with a
preceding similar study dated ___.  The chest findings are
completely unaltered and thus there is no evidence of any new or reoccurring
pulmonary infiltrate.  Heart size also unchanged and no evidence of pulmonary
vascular congestion.  The lateral pleural sinuses remain free.

IMPRESSION:  Stable chest findings, no evidence of new pneumonic infiltrate.

PA AND LATERAL CHEST, ___

HISTORY:  AML.  Following bone marrow transplant.

IMPRESSION:  PA and lateral chest compared to ___, 3:20 p.m.

FINDINGS:  Lungs clear.  Heart size normal.  No pleural abnormality. 
Mediastinal widening due primarily to fat deposition unchanged since at least
___.

INDICATION:  ___ man with AML and bone marrow transplant more than one
year ago. Evaluate for pneumonia.

COMPARISON:  CT chest of ___.  Chest radiograph of ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained through the chest without
intravenous contrast material.  Multiplanar reformatted images were generated.

CT CHEST WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:  Lungs demonstrate multifocal regions of
clustered peribronchovascular and centrilobular nodules, particularly within
the left upper lobe, lingula, and right upper lobe. Additionally, there are
adjacent foci of ground glass opacity. This is similar in degree but different
in location than on the prior study of ___. Mild bronchial wall
thickening is also seen in these regions. This is most consistent with acute
endobronchial infection. There is no focal consolidation or pleural effusions.
There is no pneumothorax. The tracheobronchial tree is patent to subsegmental
levels. There is mild dependent atelectasis.

The heart size is normal, and there is no pericardial effusion.  Scattered
lymph nodes throughout the mediastinum are unchanged since ___. There
is no axillary or hilar lymphadenopathy.

In the upper abdomen, surgical clips in the gallbladder fossa are consistent
with prior cholecystectomy.  A high-density focus within the stomach likely
reflects ingested material.  There are no gross abnormalities in the upper
abdomen, given the absence of intravenous contrast material.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  Degenerative changes are again noted throughout the
spine.  There are no worrisome lytic or sclerotic bony lesions.  Soft tissues
are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Multiple foci of clustered peribronchovascular and centrilobular nodules
in the left upper lobe, lingula and right upper lobe.  Given the change in
distribution compared to the ___ exam, this suggests endobronchial
infection, possibly atypical mycobacteria. Bronchiolitis obliterans is less
likely given the change since ___. This is not a typical pattern for drug
reaction.

2.  Diffuse bronchial wall thickening suggests acute bronchitis.

3.  No lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

4.  No interval change in hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been feeling unwell since this morning. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up with nausea and threw up—dark brown stuff. I also had a fever, around 101. I didn’t have any diarrhea or belly pain, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned joint pain making it hard to walk. Has that been worse lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been bad, but I’ve had it for months since the transplant. I’ve been on prednisone for it. But today, the nausea and fever came out of nowhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got your Rituxan infusion yesterday, correct? That could sometimes cause a reaction, but we need to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had it yesterday. Could that be why I feel so sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your fever and the brown vomit are concerning. We’ve started you on IV antibiotics—cefepime and vancomycin—just in case it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is my lung okay? I’ve had breathing issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial chest X-ray was clear, but we’re doing a CT scan to look more closely. Your oxygen level was in the 80s on room air, so we’ve given you oxygen through a nasal cannula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I do feel better with the oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the CT scan of your chest shows small nodules in both upper lobes. They weren’t there before. This suggests an infection in the airways, possibly from an atypical bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like pneumonia. We don’t see any viruses in your nasal swab, and your blood cultures haven’t grown anything yet. So we’re treating it as bacterial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics I’m on now be enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’re using broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover all possibilities. Once we know more, we might adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your respiratory virus test came back negative—no flu, RSV, or others. Blood tests also show no CMV or fungal infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a virus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look like it. The pattern on your CT scan still points to a bacterial infection, possibly atypical. We’ll keep you on the current antibiotics today and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. It might have been related to the infection or even the Rituxan. Since you’re improving, we’re confident we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your temperature has been normal since yesterday. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger too. Do I still need the IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch you to an oral antibiotic called levofloxacin. It covers the kind of bacteria we suspect. You’ll take it for 14 days at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. It won’t interact with your voriconazole or immunosuppressants. We’ll monitor your kidney function, though, since your creatinine is a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on oxygen since I got here. Will I need it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On admission, you were in the 80s on room air. Now you’re at 95% on 2 liters. We’ll wean you down and see how you do. You may need it for ambulation for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative for bacteria, fungi, and TB. That supports our decision to treat with levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no dangerous bugs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing dangerous grew. That’s reassuring. Your body is likely fighting off a community-acquired pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My joint pain is still there. Should I keep taking prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping your prednisone at 15 mg daily. It’s helping your chronic GVHD. We’ll discuss tapering with your transplant team later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on oral antibiotics. Your oxygen saturation is 97% on 1.5 liters. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full 14-day course of levofloxacin. Keep using oxygen as needed, especially when walking. And monitor for fever, shortness of breath, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are the same. We’re adding a new medication—esomeprazole—for your acid reflux. It’s called Nexium. Take it once a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heartburn lately. That might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night, you stayed at 96% on 1.5 liters of oxygen. You walked to the bathroom without trouble. We’re comfortable discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I need follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll see your oncologist and transplant team next week. They’ll review your GVHD and medications. Also, keep your primary care visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I’m going home. This stay was scary at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you responded well to treatment. The key is finishing the antibiotics and watching for any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start feeling feverish again, I’ll call my doctor or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same for nausea, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home. Your oxygen will be set at 2 liters for portability. Use it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll take good care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Remember: levofloxacin once daily for 14 days, Nexium for reflux, and keep all your other meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll follow up with my teams next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’re glad you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Nausea is gone, and I can walk without getting winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your oxygen sat is 98% on 1.5 liters. That’s a big improvement from when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Stay safe, and don’t skip those follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid crowds while on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Yes, try to avoid large gatherings and sick people. Your immune system is still recovering from the transplant and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay home as much as I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wise. And keep washing your hands and wearing a mask if you go out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my insulin as usual. My sugars have been okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep monitoring. The steroids can raise your blood sugar, so your sliding scale is still important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The home health team will set up your oxygen and check in on you. They’ll also review your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I was worried about managing everything alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. We’ve got you covered. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia and allogeneic cord blood transplant complicated by chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted with nausea, brown emesis, and fever one day after receiving Rituxan. Initial evaluation revealed hypoxia and bilateral lung crackles. A CT chest showed new peribronchovascular and centrilobular nodules, concerning for bacterial pneumonia. He was started on IV cefepime and vancomycin, then transitioned to oral levofloxacin after two days of being afebrile. Respiratory viral panel, blood cultures, and CMV testing were negative. His oxygen requirement improved from 2L to 1.5L nasal cannula, and he was discharged home on a 14-day course of levofloxacin, continued immunosuppressants, and a new prescription for esomeprazole for reflux. He was stable at discharge, with plans for outpatient follow-up.
